keys.noIdentity.body: You need one to encrypt files for a contact or share your public key. It only takes a moment — enter your master passphrase to create it.
pgpTour.what.title: What is a PGP identity?
pgpTour.what.body: A pair of two related keys: a public one, which you share, and a private one, which you keep secret. Together they let you encrypt files only you can open.
pgpTour.use.title: What does SafetyVault use it for?
pgpTour.use.body: Only to encrypt files you send or receive from a contact. Your password vault is already protected by your master passphrase — this is separate, and optional.
pgpTour.pair.title: Public vs. private
pgpTour.pair.body: Anyone can use your public key to encrypt a file for you. Only your private key can open it — never share it, not even with whoever wrote to you.
pgpTour.ready.title: Let's create it
pgpTour.ready.body: It takes a few seconds. We'll ask for your master passphrase to protect the private key — the same one you use to unlock SafetyVault.
keys.what.title: What is a keyserver?
keys.what.1: A directory on the internet where people publish their public PGP keys so others can find them by email. SafetyVault uses keys.openpgp.org, the modern verifying keyserver.
keys.what.2: Publishing requires email confirmation (a verification link is sent to the address on your key). Once verified, anyone can fetch your key by email.

tl.intro: A 2-minute, plain-language walkthrough of how your vault keeps things locked — no tech background needed.
tl.publicDesc: Share it freely. It is only used to encrypt data destined for you.
tl.privateDesc: Keep it secret. Only this key can decrypt what was locked with your public key.
tl.s1.title: You get two keys
tl.s1.body: When you create an account, SafetyVault generates two keys that belong only to you. Think of a mailbox: anyone can drop a letter in, only you have the key to take letters out.
tl.s2.title: Your passphrase guards the private key
tl.s2.body: The private key file on disk is itself encrypted with your master passphrase. No passphrase, no access — not even to us. Without it, the file is useless, even if someone copies it.
tl.s3.title: Locking a message
tl.s3.body: To send you something private, someone locks it with your public key. From that moment only your private key can open it.
tl.s4.title: The whole vault is locked too
tl.s4.body: Your passwords, notes and cards are stored as one scrambled blob. On disk it looks like meaningless noise until you unlock it. SafetyVault uses a hybrid scheme: a strong random AES-256 key (encrypted with your PGP public key) does the bulk symmetric encryption per field, and the vault as a whole is PGP-wrapped on save.
tl.s5.title: Pick a passphrase you can keep
tl.s6.title: The key directory
tl.s6.body: To encrypt a file for someone else, you need their public key. The Key management page lets you import public keys from people you trust so you can lock files addressed to them.
tl.tip1: Length wins. A 4-word passphrase like caballo correcto batería grapa is much stronger than P@ss1! and far easier to remember.
tl.tip2: Never reuse it. If a website you use is breached and you share passphrases, attackers get your vault too.
tl.tip3: Don't write it down digitally. Pen and paper in a locked drawer is fine.
tl.tip4: It is not recoverable. If you forget it, nobody — including us — can decrypt your vault.
tl.tip5: Back up the private key file. Copy private_key.asc to an offline drive.

keys.move.title: Take your identity to another device
keys.move.body: Your key pair is who you are to the people who encrypt files for you. Creating a new identity on another phone makes anything already sent to the old one unreadable. This carries the same key across.
keys.move.warning: The file holds your private key. It travels encrypted, but move it over a direct route — a cable or AirDrop — and delete it afterwards.
